summary: Internet mail uses From: for the author and Sender: for whoever handled the message, but strict protections on From: have led mailing lists to rewrite it, so it now acts more like a handling identifier. This experimental document defines an Author: header field that names the original author and is not modified by mediators. It is Experimental to gauge community interest.

eli5.summary: Mailing lists sometimes change the name on a letter. This experimental document adds a second label that always keeps the original writer's name, so it does not get changed.

questions: what is the author header field
why do mailing lists modify from
how is author different from from
subtitle: Preserving the original author when mailing lists modify the From field

tldr.problem: Mailing lists often modify the From: header to pass authentication checks, replacing the original author's address with the list address, making recipients unable to reliably identify who actually sent the message.
tldr.mechanism: The Author: header field preserves the original message author's identity with the same syntax as From:, and is not subject to modification by mailing list intermediaries.
tldr.outcome: Mail clients can now rely on Author: to identify the true author, while From: becomes an operational handle. The document is Experimental to assess community adoption.

today: RFC 9057 is an Experimental specification. Mail client vendors and mailing list operators have the specification but adoption remains to be demonstrated. The standard may transition to Standards Track if implementation and deployment are successful.

sections.title: The Problem With From
sections.content:
Internet mail has long used the From: header field to identify the message author. In the original design, the Sender: field identified who handled the message on behalf of the author. When the two were the same, Sender was omitted as redundant.

Modern email authentication systems like DMARC and SPF protect the From: field strictly to prevent spoofing. This has created a problem: when a message passes through a mailing list, the list must modify the From: field to avoid authentication failures, changing it from the original author to the list's address. The recipient's mail client then sees many messages from the same person as coming from different addresses—each mailing list address—making it impossible to reliably group or filter by author.

The Author: header field solves this by giving message authors and mailing list mediators a way to preserve the original authorship information separately from the operational From: field.
sections.eli5: When your letter goes through a mailing list, the list changes who the letter says it is from, so email security checks pass. The new Author field lets you write down who really sent it first, so it does not get forgotten.

sections.title: The Author Header Field
sections.content:
The Author: field has identical syntax and semantics to the From: field. It contains the email address and optional display name of the original message author.

Author: can be created at two points in a message's life. The author's mail client can add it when composing (with the same value as From:). More commonly, a mediator such as a mailing list adds it before modifying the From: field, preserving the author's original address. Once an Author: field exists in a message, no other entity may modify or replace it—this ensures it remains immutable end-to-end.
sections.eli5: The Author field looks the same as the From field and holds the writer's name and email. Once someone writes it down, nobody is allowed to change it.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
The RFC specifies strict rules to ensure Author: stays reliable. If an Author: field already exists, it MUST never be touched. An author's mail client MAY create one with the value from From:. A Mediator MAY create one if it does not exist, capturing the From: value before the Mediator modifies it.

This means Author: represents what the original author put in From:, frozen in place. Mail clients can now organize, filter, and display messages grouped by Author: instead of From:, giving users a consistent view of all mail from a person regardless of which list it came through.
sections.eli5: The rules say: if Author exists, leave it alone; mail programs can add it when they send; list operators can add it if it is not there. Once it is written, it stays the same forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like any identification header, Author: carries authentication and privacy risks. Mail systems should apply scrutiny comparable to From:, but the RFC notes something important: despite many real demonstrations of users being tricked by email content, there is no documented evidence that false author identification in a header field directly causes problematic behavior. The concern exists in principle, but lacks a track record of actual harm.

Security systems must distinguish Author: from From: and treat their information separately. An Author: field claiming to be from an attacker is no more dangerous than the From: field already is, because the RFC's immutability rule means an attacker cannot add a false Author: to an existing message—only the original sender can.
sections.eli5: The Author field is like other name fields in email—it can be faked, so antispam tools need to care about it. But since no one can change it after it is sent, only the real sender can put a false name in it, just like with the From field.

sections.title: Experimental Status
sections.content:
RFC 9057 is Experimental, published to gauge whether mail client vendors, mailing list operators, and end users find Author: valuable. The experiment aims to answer several questions: Will mail clients implement it? If they do, will users adopt it? Does the field create operational problems? Does it introduce new security issues?

The Experimental status is temporary; if adoption is strong and no problems emerge, a later Standards Track document could make Author: a standard part of Internet mail.
sections.eli5: This is a test: the RFC asks mail program makers to try it and see if people use it and if it causes trouble. If it works well, it can become a permanent part of email.
